problem: Existing navigation instruction generators rely on privileged inputs (panoramas, semantic maps, landmark annotations, actions, orientation) or compress vision into text, losing spatial detail. Generic MLLMs also lack explicit visual imagination and give imprecise, temporally inconsistent instructions.
motivation: Instruction generation matters for assisting visually impaired users, human-agent collaboration and hazardous environments, where only egocentric views are available. Humans mentally simulate the route between start and goal before describing it, so the paper gives an MLLM this visual imagination.
key_idea: Have a unified autoregressive MLLM (Anole-7B) imagine intermediate egocentric frames from start to goal (Navigation Visualization) and generate or refine instructions on those imagined frames, either in one pass or interleaved step by step.
insight: Predicting future frames grounds the instruction in intermediate visual evidence. Interleaving with iterative refinement beats one-pass (BLEU-4 0.32 vs 0.29 on val-unseen) at about 20% more inference time. The Token Discrepancy Loss is key for visualization: SSIM 0.52 to 0.69 and PSNR 15.35 to 20.02 versus the plain label-smoothing loss on image tokens. Context size trades off against per-frame token count under the 4096-token limit: 2 frames at 784 tokens beat 4 frames at 400 tokens.
method: Task decomposition: Navigation Visualization (predict next egocentric frame from k previous frames + goal) and Instruction Generation with Visual Cues (initial, intermediate, goal frames, optional previous instruction -> instruction).

Unified autoregressive MLLM: Anole-7B (Chameleon) with a frozen VQ image tokenizer (256x256 to 784 tokens) and BPE text tokenizer; LoRA (rank 16) on qkv projections; both subtasks interleaved in batches.
Token Discrepancy Loss L_vis: MSE distances between ground-truth token embedding and all codebook entries, weighted by the predicted token probability distribution; used for image tokens.
Label smoothing cross-entropy L_ins: for instruction text tokens, with input masking (-100 labels) so only targets are supervised.
One-Pass reasoning: roll out frames until SSIM(pred, goal) > 0.7, sample m-1 representative frames, generate the instruction once.
Interleaved reasoning: at each step predict the next frame, then update the instruction conditioned on the previous instruction and the sliding frame window, until the SSIM criterion is met.

R2R-Goal dataset: 74,737 synthetic trajectories from R2R-CE/HA-R2R (A* paths in the HA-VLN simulator, Qwen2.5-VL scene segmentation, manual review) plus 1,080 manually annotated real-world trajectories (GO Stanford, ReCon, HuRoN).

numbers_note: Metrics are on a 0-1 scale as printed (BLEU-4 etc.); SR/SPL for the usability study are also printed as fractions. The user-study scores (Interleaved 4.85, One-pass 4.52 on 1-6) are in the text only. The paper introduces its own benchmark, R2R-Goal, not a standard VLN benchmark.
results: Interleaved reasoning reaches BLEU-4 0.32 / CIDEr 0.20 on val-unseen, well above C-Instructor (0.22 / 0.19) and GPT-4o + CoT (0.09 / 0.16). Zero-shot on real-world data it gets BLEU-4 0.27 versus 0.15 for C-Instructor. Instructions also help navigators (ETPNav SR 0.34 vs human 0.36) and score 4.85/6 in a user study.
limitations: Depends on the 4096-token context of Anole-7B, forcing a trade-off between frame history and per-frame token count.
Interleaved reasoning costs ~20% more inference time; the SSIM stopping threshold (0.7) is a heuristic and imagined frames may drift.
Evaluated mostly on a self-built dataset with synthetic trajectories; real-world subset is small (1,080) and used only for testing; n-gram metrics have limited validity.
